fact: The Tree of Peace of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy: by tradition, the founding nations buried their weapons beneath one.
The state tree of Maine and of Michigan. Maine's state flower is its cone and tassel.
A member of the pea family, but one of the few that forms no nodules on its roots; most sources say it fixes no nitrogen.
source: Fire Effects Information System (U.S. Forest Service)

fact: When Dutch elm disease killed the elms that shaded so many American streets, the thornless form became one of the most planted trees to replace them.
The state tree of New Jersey, since 1950, and the provincial tree of Prince Edward Island, since 1987.
Like every oak in the red oak group, it takes two summers to ripen its acorns. White oaks ripen theirs in one.
First brought to North America in 1756, as seedlings sent from England to the Philadelphia botanist John Bartram.
Where it meets bur oak the two cross, and the hybrid has a name of its own: Schuette's oak, Quercus × schuettei.
Not every one is blue. Wild trees run from dull green to silvery blue, and the bluest in yards are grafted selections such as 'Hoopsii'.
The state tree of Rhode Island.
Its wilted or dried leaves, fallen after a storm or a pruning, are poisonous to horses.
Its range is split among several subspecies. One, the Corsican pine of Corsica and southern Italy, is a leading timber tree in Britain and France.
The name probably comes from the short, slender twigs that stick out like pins along its trunk and larger limbs; others trace it to the small pin knots those leave in its lumber.
Its lower branches often hold their dead brown leaves through the winter.
The state tree of four states: Vermont, New York, West Virginia and Wisconsin.
Its sap runs when freezing nights alternate with thawing days, which is why sugaring season falls at the end of winter.
Probably the first North American tree grown in Europe: one brought back from the St. Lawrence by Jacques Cartier's expedition is said to have grown for years in the royal garden at Fontainebleau.
The provincial tree of Manitoba, and, as Black Hills spruce, the state tree of South Dakota.
The national tree of the Czech Republic and of Slovakia.
The Christmas tree in London's Trafalgar Square is a Norway spruce, sent by the city of Oslo every year since 1947 in thanks for Britain's help in the Second World War.
Trees are male or female. The female's seeds have a fleshy coat that smells of rancid butter when it falls and rots, which is why almost all planted ginkgos are male.
Its soft, light, even-grained wood is a favorite of woodcarvers.
The state tree of New Hampshire and the provincial tree of Saskatchewan.
One parent of the London planetree, the street tree of so many cities; the other is the oriental planetree of southeastern Europe and western Asia.
It spreads by suckers from its roots, so one planted tree can become a thicket. That, with seed, is how it escapes into fields and woods.
source: Fire Effects Information System (U.S. Forest Service)

fact: A leaf-mining moth first found near Lake Ohrid in North Macedonia in 1984 has spread across Europe since, browning its leaves by midsummer.
The Major Oak in Sherwood Forest, by legend Robin Hood's shelter, is thought to be 800 to 1,000 years old.
The state tree of Louisiana.
The state tree of Oregon.
Scotland's national tree, by public vote in 2014.
The state tree of Oklahoma.
The state tree of Connecticut, Illinois and Maryland.
The state tree of Pennsylvania.
The state tree of Indiana, Kentucky and Tennessee.
Almost every one planted in the West until the 1990s came from two lots of seed that reached Harvard's Arnold Arboretum early in 1948, which it sent out to gardens around the world.
Botanists have moved it between four genera, Cupressus, Chamaecyparis, Xanthocyparis and Callitropsis, and still do not agree which it belongs in.
The state tree of Missouri and Virginia, and the state flower of North Carolina and Virginia.
It was Kentucky's state tree from 1976 to 1994, when the tulip poplar got the title back.
Despite its common name, mountain ash is not an ash: it is in the rose family, with apples and cherries.
The provincial tree of New Brunswick.
The state tree of Minnesota, where it is called Norway pine.
Never a dominant tree of the forest: it grows scattered among sugar maple, beech and other hardwoods and seldom forms pure stands.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

fact: Its flowers open from late summer, among the last nectar of the year for bees and hoverflies, and its black berries, rich in fat, ripen through the winter as food for blackbirds and thrushes.
On Ohio stream bottoms made too acid by coal-mine drainage for other bottomland trees, it is the tree that moves in and takes over. It is planted to reclaim strip mines.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Built for floods: in one study its seedlings survived 30 days under water, growing new roots from the drowned stem.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Apple orchards plant crabapples among their trees as pollinizers: most apples cannot set fruit with their own pollen, and a crab in bloom at the same time supplies it.
Crabapples serve as rootstocks for orchard apples. Siberian crabapple roots, for one, give the trees grafted on them the cold hardiness to fruit in the far north.
In Norway, bark bread was a famine food until the Napoleonic Wars. A bishop of Bergen recommended elm bark for it, because it held the crumbly loaves together.
The elms along the Mall in New York's Central Park are one of the largest and last remaining stands of American elm in North America.
The Canadian city of Saskatoon takes its name from the Cree word for the fruit of one serviceberry, misâskwatômina.
One kind of pemmican, the Native American food of minced dried meat and fat, was flavored with its berries.
Ash belongs to the olive family, with olives and lilacs.
Its wood is strong and springy, used for tool handles, and Fender has built electric guitar bodies of ash since 1950.
Most planted ones are nursery-made: the parents are crossed on purpose and the best seedlings selected and named, rather than wild hybrids being dug up.
Relatively easy to transplant, it has become a popular landscape tree in recent years.
In Europe its hard, pale wood is used for furniture and for turning.
Planted far from its Rocky Mountain home, it has escaped from plantings in several northeastern states, Maine and New York among them.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

fact: Some live more than 500 years. The oldest known, in Uşak province in western Turkey, is thought to be about 1,000.
The usual wood for the ribs, gunwales and other main parts of a birchbark canoe.
The northernmost tree in North America, reaching just past 69°N in the delta of the Mackenzie River.
Aachen's Forster Linde, a littleleaf linden, is thought to be about 1,000 years old, though no old linden can be dated exactly: their hearts rot away, taking the rings with them.
Most of Stradivari's violin tops, a 2026 tree-ring study found, were Norway spruce grown high in the Alps, where the cold made for many narrow rings.
In Korea it is the classic village guardian tree, planted at the heart of villages for protection, and many old ones are protected as natural monuments.
Besides Dutch elm disease, it resists the elm leaf beetle, an insect that strips the leaves of elms.
Bees make an excellent, mildly spicy honey from its flowers.
Long thought extinct in the wild. A few stands in the mountains of southwestern China may be the last wild survivors; every other ginkgo descends from trees people planted.
Its sap is sweet, but sugarmakers seldom tap it: it is usually less sugary than sugar maple's, so takes more boiling, and its buds break early, which cuts the season short.
Its seeds often lie in the ground a full extra year, sprouting only in the second spring after they fall.
source: Woody Plant Seed Manual (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Pure stands of paper birch burn far less often than the mixed forest around them, only in unusually dry years.
source: USDA Forest Service Climate Change Tree Atlas

fact: There are just five species of Thuja: two in North America and three in eastern Asia.
The popular hedge 'Green Giant' can grow 3 to 4 feet a year in good conditions.
Once widely planted as a city shade tree, it has largely given way to the London planetree, which resists the leaf disease anthracnose that disfigures it.
Named for Jean Robin, herbalist to King Henry IV of France. A black locust in Paris's Square René-Viviani, said to have been planted by him around 1601, is the oldest tree in the city.
The scars its leaves leave on the twigs are shaped like horseshoes, complete with seven nails.
Larches dominate the boreal forests of Siberia and Canada. They are Russia's most abundant trees, the main tree on over a third of its forest land.
source: Abaimov, Permafrost Ecosystems: Siberian Larch Forests (Springer, 2010)

fact: No tree genus grows farther north: in North America and Siberia larches reach the edge of the tundra.
About 35 kinds of gall grow on it, among them the oak apple, a spongy ball that a tiny wasp makes the tree grow from a bud.
The oldest known, along the Black River in North Carolina, is at least 2,624 years old: the oldest living tree in eastern North America.
Its acorns are the largest of any native oak, hence macrocarpa, large fruit.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

fact: It bears big acorn crops only every few years. The glut is more than squirrels, deer and jays can eat, so some acorns survive to sprout: a strategy called masting.
From about 40 or 50 years old a Lombardy poplar starts shedding branches and blows over easily, and each one that falls exposes the next, so whole rows can go down like dominoes.
Its species, the black poplar, is one of Britain's rarest native trees: only about 7,000 grow wild there, and only some 600 of them are female.
Many hawthorns set seed without pollination, each copying itself, so the genus splinters into near-identical lines. Botanists have counted anywhere from about 150 to over 1,000 species.
Its wood seldom rots, so farmers planted it for fence posts. It was tried, less successfully, for railroad ties.
Coast Douglas firs commonly live more than 500 years, and now and then more than 1,000.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: In subarctic Lapland its needles stay on the tree up to nine years, and the oldest recorded trees there, in northern Finland, are over 760 years old.
Its nuts fed much of the eastern forest each fall: deer, wild turkeys and, before it went extinct, the passenger pigeon.
Big American chestnuts planted by settlers still grow in the West, in Sherwood, Oregon, for one, beyond the reach of the blight that killed the eastern trees.
Its nuts make up about a tenth of the eastern fox squirrel's diet.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Even its ground shells are put to use: as a non-slip agent in tires, to blast off paint, and in smokestack scrubbers.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Its nectar sits too deep for short-tongued bees. Long-tongued bees, carpenter bees and blueberry bees among them, do its pollinating.
Its bark was once a main source of tannin for tanning leather.
Maryland's Wye Oak, a white oak thought to be over 450 years old, stood until a thunderstorm brought it down in 2002.
Native Americans hollowed its trunks into dugout canoes so often that early settlers west of the Appalachians called it canoewood. A big one could carry twenty people.
Besides heat and drought, it stands city air, pollution and compacted soil, which makes it a good street tree.
The first living tree known to science grew beside a village shrine in Hubei, where villagers called it shui-shan, water fir.
Fossils of its ancestor turn up in Alaska and Greenland, far north of where sweetgum grows today.
Its wood goes into furniture, crates and plywood veneer, and once went into the cabinets of radios, televisions and phonographs.
Its catkins are the most important food of ruffed grouse from late fall to early spring.
Beechnuts were a main food of the passenger pigeon, and clearing the beech and oak forests is thought to have helped drive the bird extinct.
Its nuts feed a long list of animals: black bears, deer, wild turkeys, ruffed grouse, raccoons, foxes, squirrels and porcupines among them.
A favorite of bonsai growers: its small leaves get smaller still, and its twigs branch more finely, when it is pruned and pinched.
Nurseries can graft it onto ash roots.

The emerald ash borer, the beetle killing North America's ashes, was found in white fringetrees in Ohio in 2014 and Illinois in 2015. Of three non-ash trees tested, it was the only one the beetle could grow up in.
Its leaves, boiled with iron sulphate, give a black dye.
The largest North American birch.
The provincial tree of Quebec.
To many noses its flowers smell of rotting fish.
Its fast growth and tight, upright forks make 'Bradford' trees prone to splitting apart in storms and under ice.
Copper beeches, its purple-leaved form, arose as natural mutants in several parts of Europe, and were known in Germany before 1488.
It flowers in fall, from late September to late November and sometimes into December.
There are more than 7,500 named varieties of apple.
Its flowers open before the leaves, making it one of the first nectar sources for bees in spring, and maples feed the caterpillars of the imperial moth.
Its roots run shallow and far: they lift driveways and sidewalks and find their way into septic systems and drains.
Its seeds are spread mainly by birds, and big crops come only every three to five years.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Its small fruits are edible, mild raw or cooked, and can be made into jelly or tea; birds and squirrels eat them through the winter.
Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the gray hairstreak, red-spotted purple and viceroy butterflies.
It stands clay, dry and alkaline soils and road salt, so it is often planted along North American streets.
Its flowers draw butterflies and even hummingbirds, and deer usually leave it alone.
The name catalpa comes from the Muscogee (Creek) name for the tree, kutuhlpa, "winged head".
In Japan it is ōyamazakura, the "great mountain cherry", for flowers larger than the common mountain cherry's, and also beni-yamazakura, "red mountain cherry", for their deeper color.
Its pea-sized cherries ripen purple-black in summer and are too bitter to eat off the tree.
A silver linden in Copou Park in Iași, Romania, some 450 to 540 years old, is a national landmark: the poet Mihai Eminescu is said to have written some of his best work beneath it.
Its wood is white, hard and strong, used for furniture and turning, and prized for musical instruments, harps above all.
It belongs to the cashew family, with mango, pistachio, sumac and poison ivy, and its resinous sap can give a rash to people sensitive to poison ivy.
Its nutlets feed songbirds, wild turkeys and quail, and the witches'-brooms common on its branches shelter many insects.
Its soft wood turns easily, and was made into spools, clothespins and other small woodenware.
Its twigs are winter browse for snowshoe hare, moose and white-tailed deer, and in Maine its thickets hide bobcats and hares.
Canada's oldest known tree was one of these, in the Caren Range of British Columbia: about 1,800 years old when it was felled in 1980.
Its light, soft wood goes mostly to pulp and particleboard, and into matches, chopsticks, pallets and hockey sticks.
It is a favorite food of the spongy moth, whose caterpillars can strip it bare; a stand weakened that way often dies of root rot after.
Its acorns feed squirrels and birds, and its leaves the caterpillars of the imperial moth and banded hairstreak.
Where it meets black oak it crosses with it; the hybrid is called Lea's oak.
Its many named forms run from 'Densiformis', a mound 3 to 4 feet tall, to 'Hicksii', a column up to 20 feet, raised at Hicks Nurseries on Long Island.
It is poisonous to horses, dogs and cats as well as people, yet birds eat its red arils and spread the seeds.
Its sap is sugary, and the Plains peoples boiled it into syrup, though it is less sweet than sugar maple's.
Its young saplings, with three ragged leaflets, are often mistaken for poison ivy; boxelder's leaves grow in opposite pairs, poison ivy's one at a time.
One of the few trees that colors well even in shade, though more softly than in sun.
Described in 1901, it was not brought into cultivation until 1923, and is still hard to find in nurseries.
It and one other species make up a family of their own, whose fossils go back to the last age of the dinosaurs, in North America, Europe and Asia.
Trees are male or female. The males flower before the leaves come out, the females as they open; both flowers are small and easy to miss.
Both its names mean alder: clethra is the Greek for alder, alnifolia "with leaves like alder's". Another old name is white alder, though the two are not related.
It is often planted along streams and ponds to hold the banks against erosion, as it stands both short floods and short droughts once settled.
Its fruit is edible: the sweet pulp tastes something like ripe persimmon, the rind is tough and bitter, and it is sometimes made into wine. Most are left for the birds.
Rutgers University crossed it with the native flowering dogwood to breed disease-resistant hybrids, Cornus × rutgersensis.

The grove on Longwood Mall in Brookline, Massachusetts, planted by David Sears in the 1840s, is thought to be the oldest stand of European beeches in the United States; beech leaf disease now threatens it.
Its strong, shock-resistant wood is sold together with white ash's as "white ash", for tool handles, baseball bats and electric guitar bodies.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Tadpoles feed on the leaves that fall into ponds, and ash leaves, low in tannins, suit them well; in one study, tadpoles raised on the maple leaves now replacing ash survived less well and grew smaller.
French settlers in Canada called it chicot, "stubby", for its thick twigs and late leaves.
Pond's, the cosmetics brand, began in 1846 as Pond's Extract, a witch hazel remedy made by the pharmacist Theron Pond of Utica, New York.
The word apple comes from Old English æppel, which meant any fruit; the pineapple keeps that older sense.
It harbors crown rust, a fungus that attacks oats, and is the main winter host in North America of the soybean aphid, a pest of soybeans.
It leafs out before the native shrubs and shades them out, and its rich leaf litter feeds invasive European earthworms, which strip the forest floor bare.
Its worst enemy is the spruce budworm, which prefers it to spruce despite the name; three years' defoliation in an outbreak can kill three-quarters of a tree's fine roots.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Once dismissed by loggers as a weed tree, it is now one of the most important commercial softwoods of the West.
source: Wikipedia; Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: It is host to two parasitic mistletoes, and the swellings dwarf mistletoe raises on its trunk weaken the lumber cut from it.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Its name griseum, "gray", probably refers to the silvery undersides of its leaves, not its coppery bark.
Most trees in western gardens descend from a few early introductions, so in 2015 an expedition went to China to collect its seed and widen the stock.
Its heavy wood is used for furniture, cabinets and millwork, and is usually sold with yellow birch, not told apart.
source: Wikipedia; Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the mourning cloak butterfly, and a leafcutter bee cuts pieces from them to line its nest.
Box Hill in Surrey is named for it: the hill holds the largest native box woodland in England.
The box tree moth, from East Asia, settled in Europe in 2007, and its caterpillars now strip boxwoods across the continent.
Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the hackberry emperor and question mark butterflies.
Its pea-sized berries are edible and ripen in September; the Omaha ate them as they were, and the Dakota pounded them, seeds and all, to season meat.
Its yellow heartwood is used in small amounts for fine furniture, gunstocks and woodturning.
Prune it only in summer: cut in winter or spring, it bleeds sap heavily.
Its other old names are snowdrop-tree and opossum-wood.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Its soft, close-grained wood is a favorite for crafts; squirrels eat its seeds, and bees make honey from its flowers.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Dye from its bark colored the paper of Buddhist sutras across East Asia, the Diamond Sutra among them.
Trees are male or female, and only the females bear the black fruits that birds carry off; it is now listed as invasive in Illinois, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia.
Its fruit is edible raw and made into jelly, and the juice was once used to flavor rum and brandy, which gives it the name rum cherry.
source: Wikipedia; Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Planted in western and central Europe in the mid-1900s, it has run wild there and is now an invasive weed of European forests.
Its name aucuparia means "bird-catching": fowlers baited their traps with the berries.
Its name pseudocamellia means "false camellia", and in Japanese it is natsutsubaki, "summer camellia".
In Japan it is also called shara: from the 1700s it stood in at temples for the sal tree, sacred in Buddhism, which does not grow there.
The purple lilac is New Hampshire's state flower, chosen as "symbolic of that hardy character of the men and women of the Granite State".
Between 1876 and 1927 one French nursery, Victor Lemoine's in Nancy, introduced more than 150 named lilacs, many still sold today.
In the Western Caucasus Reserve, some are reported to top 250 feet, which would make them the tallest trees in Europe.
In parts of Europe it is planted in forests to replace trees expected to decline as the climate warms.
In Minoh, near Osaka, its leaves are made into momiji tempura: salted for a year, then coated in a sweet batter with sesame and fried.
The Swedish botanist Carl Peter Thunberg drew and named it in Japan in the 1780s, for its hand-shaped leaves; the first tree reached Britain in 1821.
It was the classic hedge of French formal gardens: the clipped walls of the bosquets at Versailles are hornbeam.
Its wood made butchers' chopping blocks and piano hammers, and it burns well, as firewood and as charcoal.
Ise Grand Shrine, Shinto's holiest, is rebuilt every 20 years from hinoki grown in Kiso, where the trees are called go-shinboku, "divine trees".
The lemon-scented oil from its wood goes into perfumes, soaps and shampoos, and the wood into stick incense.
Its fruits feed at least eleven kinds of birds, black bears, chipmunks, deer and rabbits, and beavers eat its branches near water.
It is prone to golden canker, a fungus that kills branches, especially when heat or drought stresses the plant.
Its name mas, "male", set it apart from the dogberry, the "female" cornel, as John Gerard's Herbal of 1597 has it.
Its tart fruit is stewed into kompot in Bulgaria, made into a spirit in Romania and Moldova, pickled in Azerbaijan, and dried and salted as a sour seasoning in Iran.
Because it does not sucker, it is used as a single-stemmed rootstock for grafting the common hazel.
Its nuts were sold as Turkish or Constantinople nuts, and squirrels are very fond of them.
Its dried fruit, senjed, is one of the seven items on the haft-sin table set out for Nowruz, the Persian new year, where it stands for love.
It starts to flower and fruit at only three years old, one reason it spreads so fast.
Oregon and Washington list it as a noxious weed and ban its sale.
Its late, nectar-rich flowers draw bees and migrating monarch butterflies in September, and in North America hummingbirds too.
The first trees planted in the West, at the Arnold Arboretum in 1980, are still alive more than 40 years on.
Its genus honors Richard Kolkwitz, a Berlin professor of botany, and amabilis means "lovely".
Wilson sent its seed to Veitch Nurseries in Exeter, England, where it first flowered in 1910, nine years later.
It is the favorite food of the spicebush swallowtail, whose young caterpillars look like bird droppings and hide in leaves they fold shut with silk.
Another name is wild allspice, and its young leaves and twigs make a spicy tea.
It is the type species of Magnolia: the species to which the genus name, and so the name of the whole magnolia family, is formally tied.
Its black seeds hang out of the ripe pink fruit on threads, in a thin red coat; birds swallow them, digest the coat and drop the seeds elsewhere.
Its catkins fling out their pollen at more than half the speed of sound, one of the fastest movements known in plants.
Its fibrous bark has long been made into paper, and more recently into rayon.
In Japan its fibers are woven into a cloth called bashōfu.
It needs 12 to 24 months of warmth to flower, so in the North it blooms only if brought indoors in a pot and kept growing through the winter.
The name tupelo comes from the Creek words ito, "tree", and opilwa, "swamp".
Its small flowers are rich in nectar and a major source of wild honey; beekeepers once used its hollow trunks as hives, called bee gums.
It is also sold as Japanese andromeda, from the genus it used to be placed in.
Its genus is named for Pieria, the place in Greece that myth makes the home of the Muses.
It is one of the most widely planted trees in the northern United States and Canada.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Like other cherries, its leaves, stems and seeds are poisonous to dogs, cats and horses.
Its small dark fruits are edible, though strong-tasting, and birds take them.
Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the giant swallowtail, North America's largest butterfly.
It has a long list of other names, among them hoptree, stinking prairie bush, quinine tree and ague bark.
Its acorns take about 18 months to ripen, and the kernels are very bitter.
Its wood is used for fence posts, firewood and general building.
It is called cow oak because cattle eat its large, sweet acorns, as do deer, squirrels, hogs and black bears.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: It is also called basket oak: its wood splits into long, thin, flexible strips for weaving baskets.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Its dried, ground leaves are filé powder, which thickens and flavors Louisiana gumbo.
Its root was one of the first exports from North America to Europe, shipped from as early as 1609.
Vermont lists it as a threatened plant, and Ontario as endangered.
It is named for Richard Maack, a 19th-century Russian naturalist and explorer who found it in the Amur River valley, on the border of Siberia and China.
Its pea-like flowers smell of vanilla, and its flat seed pods, 2 to 4 inches long, follow in fall.
Rare in the wild, it is listed as threatened in North Carolina and endangered in Arkansas and Ohio; its trees grow far apart and set few good seeds.
Butterflies and hummingbirds visit its flowers, and birds and small mammals eat its red seeds.
It is named for John Fraser (1750–1811), the Scottish plant collector who explored these mountains.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: The balsam woolly adelgid, an invasive insect first recorded in its wild stands in 1957, has devastated them, and the species is now listed as endangered.
David Douglas found it near the mouth of the Columbia River in 1825, and later brought it into British gardens.
Its lumber goes into framing, flooring and paper.
It reached Japan in the early 1700s, and its Japanese name, tōkaede, means "Chinese maple".
Its species name honors Heinrich Bürger, a 19th-century German botanist.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: In Japan and elsewhere it is grown as bonsai.
Pruning can make it a single-trunked small tree or a many-stemmed shrub, and it is one of the hardiest maples, best where summers are cool.
The Morton Arboretum near Chicago selected a dense, even form, 'Morton', sold as State Street maple.
The botanist Kingo Miyabe found it on a stop during a train ride; it was described in 1888 and reached Germany the same year.
source: Oregon State University; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Its timber is sold with sugar maple's as "hard maple".
Small leafy stipules at the base of each leaf stalk tell it from sugar maple.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: In Britain it is known simply as sycamore, and also as great maple and harewood, the name its wood is sold under for veneer.
Its pale, odorless wood has long been the choice for kitchenware such as cutting boards and bowls, and its rare wavy-grained timber for violins.
It is also called purplebloom maple: its flowers have reddish-purple sepals around cream petals and open before the leaves.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; Boone County Arboretum

fact: Another name for it is Keijo maple, after Keijō, the name Seoul went by under Japanese rule.
Its name is often misspelled Tartar or Tartarian maple.
It has escaped and become invasive in parts of the Midwest.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Its name truncatum, "cut off square", refers to the straight base of its leaves.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Crossed with Norway maple, it gave 'Keithsform', sold as Norwegian Sunset.
Its name pedatum, "like a bird's foot", describes how the frond forks.
It also grows in eastern Asia; Asa Gray counted it among the plants shared by Japan and North America.
Native Americans ate its seeds after roasting them and leaching out the poison in water for several days.
source: NC State Extension; Oregon State University; Wikipedia

fact: Its leaves resist disease better than other buckeyes'.
Ohio State University took "Buckeyes" as its official nickname in 1950.
Native Americans ground the nuts and put them in streams to stun fish.
Its August flowers draw butterflies, bees and hummingbirds.
It is poisonous to people, dogs, cats and horses if eaten.
Crossed with horse chestnut, it gave the red horsechestnut, which takes its red flowers from this parent.
Its flower clusters last about a month and draw hummingbirds and bees; squirrels eat the seeds.
Its best-known form, 'Autumn Splendor', was raised by the University of Minnesota from seed sent by the Morton Arboretum and released in 1980.
source: University of Minnesota; Chicago Botanic Garden

fact: The University of Minnesota lists 'Autumn Splendor' among shade trees that resist leaf scorch, though it still needs water in a drought.
source: University of Minnesota; North Dakota State University

fact: Unusually for a hybrid, it comes true from seed: its chromosomes doubled at some point, making it fertile.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

fact: Its brightest form, 'Briotii', was named in 1858 for Pierre Briot, head gardener of the state gardens at the Trianon, Versailles.
It is the favorite host of the spotted lanternfly, an invasive insect from Asia, which makes the tree's spread worse.
In China and abroad it has been grown to feed the ailanthus silkmoth, whose cocoons give a coarse silk.
